rationale:
Evidence. Iteration 9 (wheel_track 0.14, otherwise iteration 8) scored 98.24, the best raced design so far, up from 85.47. Oval progress rose from 0.268 to 0.373 and the oval finish rate was 1 in 20 trials. S-bend progress held at 0.160 and its max_error fell only slightly, from 0.0606 to 0.0603. Slalom progress fell from 0.113 to 0.101, its max_error rose from 0.065 to 0.0623, and line loss returned (0.6 events per trial). Oval max_error was unchanged at 0.061. Every trial still ends off_track, and max_error has stayed pinned at 0.060 to 0.065 across iterations 0 to 9.

Decision. The approved contingency applies. max_error did not drop to 0.060 or below on oval or s-bend, and slalom progress fell clearly below 0.113. So the next single-variable test is geometry.wheel_track = 0.10 m, with everything else as iteration 9. Iteration 9 is kept as the fallback. I am not moving base_speed in this iteration, because the drivetrain result is not yet clear.

Expected result. A narrower track gives more turn per wheel difference. That should restore slalom steering authority and the line-loss recovery on tight bends. If the constant-bias explanation holds, the oval and s-bend max_error may rise, so the oval finish rate could fall. I expect the score to move either way by a moderate amount.

Hypotheses. H1: the motor-mismatch bias is the drift source, and at 0.10 m the slalom line loss clears while max_error stays near 0.060 on oval and s-bend. H2: max_error stays at 0.061 or above at both 0.14 and 0.10, which would show the drivetrain is not the cause. The next step would then be sensor geometry, such as sensor_size 0.012 at the wide span, in the final iteration.

Measurements wanted: max_error, line_loss_events, progress, completion and steering_oscillation per track, to compare against iteration 9 and against iteration 8.
